content: Licensed Practical Nurses (LPNs), also referred to as Licensed Vocational Nurses (LVNs) in California and Texas, and Registered Practical Nurses (RPNs) in Ontario, are healthcare professionals who provide essential nursing care. In Australia, they are known as Enrolled Nurses (ENs), while in the United Kingdom, they are referred to as State Enrolled Nurses (SENs). In the United States, LPNs typically undergo 12 months to 2 years of training, which includes coursework in anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology, pharmacology, and practical patient care. They are required to pass the National Council Licensure Examination for Practical Nurses (NCLEX-PN) and periodically renew their licenses. LPNs are qualified to perform both simple and complex medical procedures but must work under the supervision of a Registered Nurse (RN) or a physician. They are authorized to administer most medications, except for intravenous (IV) push medications, and are responsible for monitoring patient responses to medications, providing wound care, measuring vital signs (such as blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, and oxygen saturation), maintaining patient records, assisting in patient care planning, and performing sterile and isolation procedures. They may also collect samples for laboratory testing and provide consistent, high-quality care. LPNs work in various healthcare settings, including clinics, hospitals, long-term care facilities, and private home health care. In long-term care facilities, they may supervise nursing assistants and orderlies. To become an LPN, individuals must have at least a high school diploma, graduate from an approved practical nursing program, and meet state board requirements, which often include a clean criminal record. The first formal training for practical nurses began in 1892 at the Young Women’s Christian Association in New York City, with the first official program offered at the Ballard School in 1893. By 1955, all U.S. states required licensure for LPNs. Today, LPN training is typically college-based. In the United Kingdom, the State Enrolled Nurse (SEN) qualification is no longer available. Before the implementation of Project 2000, which restructured nurse education in the mid-1990s, SEN students completed 12 months of training similar to that of State Registered Nurses (SRNs, now known as Level One Nurses), followed by an additional 12 months of training before taking SEN exams. Experienced auxiliary nurses were sometimes allowed to take the SEN exams without further training, and SRN trainees who failed their exams after three attempts could also register as SENs. Although no new SENs are trained in the UK, the Nursing and Midwifery Council allows individuals from similar roles abroad to register as Level Two Nurses. Historically, there was a clear distinction between SENs and SRNs, marked by differences in uniform color and responsibilities. However, this divide has diminished over time due to the declining number of SENs in practice. Many SENs performed duties similar to Level One Nurses, such as managing wards unsupervised at night. The discontinuation of the SEN role is viewed by some as a loss of a balanced staffing model, though concerns about potential gaps in clinical excellence were also raised. Auxiliary nurses in the UK, also known as nursing assistants, healthcare assistants, or clinical support workers, have taken on tasks traditionally performed by registered nurses, such as taking blood samples, changing dressings, and recording electrocardiograms (ECGs). Recent discussions have considered creating a separate part of the nursing register for these staff members, which would have significant implications for professional accountability, pay, working conditions, and logistics. Currently, auxiliary nurses work under the supervision of registered nurses, who are accountable for their actions. In Australia, Enrolled Nurses (ENs) typically complete 12 months of training, including 14 weeks of theoretical instruction at Technical and Further Education (TAFE) colleges, followed by practical experience in hospital wards. Many ENs eventually pursue further education to become Registered Nurses (RNs), though a significant number remain as ENs in public and private hospitals and nursing homes. The role of ENs has expanded in recent years due to a shortage of RNs in the public healthcare system. In 2004, a Medication Endorsement certificate was introduced, allowing ENs to administer most oral medications (excluding drugs of addiction) and some intravenous (IV) medications and fluids, as well as intramuscular and subcutaneous injections. Endorsed Enrolled Nurses (EENs) can also check certain medications with an RN but are not permitted to participate in daily drug counts. ENs in public hospitals are often allowed to perform ECGs, collect pathology specimens, and manage patient loads under RN supervision.
